title: Menno Simons
hook: a Dutch priest who joined the Anabaptists and gave the Mennonites his name

segments.voice: Last time: Felix Manz, drowned in Zurich, and the name Anabaptist. Your line was the peaceable kingdom.

A village priest in Friesland, in the north of the Netherlands, is saying Mass. He holds up the bread, and a doubt he can't shake rises with it. He keeps his post and his comfortable life. He reads the New Testament on the side, and the doubts grow. Then news comes that a group of Anabaptists has been killed, and tradition says his own brother was among them. Men who died for what they believed, he writes, while he stayed safe and said nothing. That thought won't leave him alone. His name is Menno Simons, and a whole family of churches still carries it.

Menno left the priesthood and joined the scattered, hunted Anabaptists of the Low Countries. He didn't start their movement; he came into it and became one of its shepherds. And he chose its peaceful side. Some who carried the Anabaptist name had turned to violence. Menno taught that Christ's followers do not take up the sword at all. From then on he lived on the move with his family, writing, preaching and baptizing believers, with authorities hunting him. His writings carried a verse from Paul, in the King James wording: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." Everything had to stand on that. Those who followed his teaching came to be called Mennonites, after him. Then there's the passage his line comes from. In paraphrase, Menno wrote that true evangelical faith cannot lie dormant. It clothes the naked. It feeds the hungry. It comforts the sorrowful. It shelters the destitute. It serves even those who harm it. It binds up what is wounded. Faith, for Menno, gets up and does things. That fits the letter of James: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." Lutheran, Catholic, Reformed and Mennonite teachers put faith and works together in different ways. But Menno's list is about bread and blankets, and it came from a man who spent years with nowhere safe to sleep.

Look honestly at the day ahead and find one thing you could do without: a purchase you don't need, a second helping, an hour of scrolling. Then pick one thing from Menno's list to put in its place, clothes set aside to give, food for someone hungry, a word for someone sad. If you pray, offer that small trade to God; if you don't, hold the choice quietly and let it settle.
Menno Simons. A Dutch priest who joined the peaceful Anabaptists and became a leader of the churches now called Mennonite.
Your line: true faith cannot lie dormant. It gets up, and it feeds and clothes. That's day eight hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Mennonite churches, named after Menno Simons, baptize believers, practice nonviolence and simple living, and are known for relief work such as sharing food, clothing and shelter.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts. The carry is the index line; the passage it comes from is paraphrased because the common English versions are modern translations.

Menno's own account (doubts about the bread while saying Mass; reading the New Testament; the death of a group of Anabaptists, often identified as the Old Cloister group, with his brother Pieter among them; his feeling that he lived comfortably while they died) is paraphrased; confirm the brother detail and the wording 'as he later remembers it'.
'His writings carried a verse from Paul' refers to 1 Corinthians 3:11 used as a motto on his title pages; confirm.
'Some who carried the Anabaptist name had turned to violence' alludes to Münster; confirm the framing is fair.
